text: Isaac Newton explained why everything that goes up must come down. Then he lost a fortune betting it wouldn't.
London, seventeen twenty. Newton is seventy-seven, and runs the Royal Mint. He literally makes England's money.
Everyone is buying shares of the South Sea Company. By spring, the price has nearly tripled.
Newton sells in April, and walks away twenty thousand pounds richer.
But the price keeps climbing. And his friends keep getting richer.
In June, the smartest man in Europe can't take it anymore. He buys back in, with almost everything he owns.
In August, one share hits a thousand pounds. In September, it falls off a cliff.
Luckily, Newton had sold early. Unluckily, he also bought back late.
A bubble is like a ball thrown in the air. It only rises while someone keeps pushing. Here, the push was new buyers. When they ran out, gravity took over.
Parliament locked the finance minister in the Tower of London, the same fortress where Newton made the coins.
Newton lost all his profit, and then some. He wrote that the South Sea left his pockets empty.
So if the man who explained gravity couldn't time the market, maybe you don't need to either.
